{{Short description|Genus of theropod dinosaur}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Late Cretaceous]], {{fossilrange|Maastrichtian|Maastrichtian|late [[Maastrichtian]]}} | image = Infernogallus jamesi (holotype, ROM VP 65050).png | image_caption = Holotype specimen (top) and reconstructed skeleton (bottom) with a [[histological]] cross-section of the leg bone | display_parents = 2 | genus = Infernogallus | parent_authority = Funston et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] | species = jamesi | authority = Funston et al., 2026 }} '''''Infernogallus''''' ({{lit|Hell chicken}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[oviraptorosaurian]] theropod dinosaur in the family [[Caenagnathidae]], known from multiple localities in the [[Late Cretaceous]] ([[Maastrichtian]] age) [[Hell Creek Formation]] of the United States. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Infernogallus jamesi''''', known from a partial articulated skull and skeleton and several isolated cranial remains. With an estimated body mass of around {{cvt|12|kg|lb}}, it is a small caenagnathid. The skull of the [[holotype]] specimen is the first nearly complete and articulated skull discovered for a caenagnathid. It shows a reorganization of jaw muscles that may be an adaptation for [[Frugivore|fruit eating]], similar to some modern parrots but unique among non-avian theropods. == Discovery and naming == [[File:Infernogallus jamesi (type locality).png|thumb|left|upright|Describing author [[David C. Evans (paleontologist)|David C. Evans]] at the [[Type locality (biology)|type locality]]]] The ''Infernogallus'' fossil material was discovered in outcrops of the [[Hell Creek Formation]] distributed throughout the [[Great Plains]] region of the United States. Five specimens are known, collected by different research groups at different times. In July 2011, C. Phipps collected a partial, articulated skeleton on private land in northwestern [[Garfield County, Montana]]. The specimen, which is preserved within a [[sandstone]] [[concretion]], underwent initial [[fossil preparation|preparation]] shortly following its excavation, after which it was acquired by the [[Royal Ontario Museum]] (ROM; [[Ontario]], Canada), where preparation was finished. Now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen ROM VP 65050, it consists of a nearly complete skull and mandible, a complete series of {{dinogloss|cervicals|cervical (neck)}} and {{dinogloss|dorsals|dorsal (trunk)}} vertebrae, the right {{dinogloss|pectoral girdle}} and forelimb, and part of the {{dinogloss|pelvis}} and right hindlimb. Since the block preserving the specimen was separated into four smaller pieces, some regions are now missing, such as the part of the {{dinogloss|scapula}} and elbow region. Two additional ROM specimens, comprising partial lower jaw remains, were collected in south-central Garfield County. They include ROM VP 64193, the fused partial left and right dentaries, and ROM VP 64194, an {{dinogloss|articular}}-{{dinogloss|surangular}}-{{dinogloss|coronoid}} complex. Their similarity in size and preservation style suggests they likely belong to a single individual. ROM VP 88690, a pair of {{dinogloss|pterygoids}} (palate bones), was collected near [[Faith, South Dakota]], after which the ROM acquired it in 2015. In 2019, Denver Fowler collected a pair of fused, partial dentaries from a microvertebrate accumulation in southwestern [[Bowman County, North Dakota]] (Mud Buttes area). It is now accessioned as North Dakota Geological Survey (NDGS) 4351. These additional pairs of dentaries are better preserved than those of the 2011 specimen, wherein the dentaries are quite crushed. In July 2026, Bazzana-Adams and colleagues used [[CT scan]]s to describe the [[inner ear]] anatomy of ROM VP 65050 (then unnamed) and two other caenagnathid specimens. In October 2026, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Infernogallus jamesi'' as a new genus and species of caenagnathid theropod based on these fossil remains, designating ROM VP 65050 as the [[holotype]] specimen. ROM VP 64193, 64194, and 88690 and NDGS 4351 were assigned to this species as [[paratype]]s. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Infernogallus'', is derived from the [[Latin]] words {{lang|la|[[:wikt:īnfernus|īnfernus]]}}, referring to {{gloss|Hell}}, and {{lang|la|[[:wikt:gallus#Noun_3|gallus]]}}, meaning {{gloss|(male) chicken}}. This alludes to both the discovery of this taxon in the Hell Creek Formation and its small, superficially bird-like form. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''jamesi'', honors James William Boyd, the grandfather of Clint Boyd (one of the describing authors), who inspired his interest in paleontology. The holotype skull of ''I. jamesi'' is the first articulated and nearly complete skull discovered for a caenagnathid oviraptorosaur. The contemporary ''Anzu'' preserves the next best skull, but is only known from disarticulated and incomplete remains. Other caenagnathids with cranial material (''[[Apatoraptor]]'', ''[[Elmisaurus]]'', and ''[[Epichirostenotes]]'') are even more fragmentary. As such, the skull of ''Infernogallus'' offers the first detailed look at the full skull of members of this clade. The significance of this discovery was emphasized by paleontologists [[Stephen L. Brusatte|Stephen Brusatte]] and Case Vincent Miller when interviewed about the publication. == Description == [[File:Infernogallus Size Comparison.svg|thumb|Size compared to a human]] As a caenagnathid, ''Infernogallus'' is a birdlike [[theropod]] with a toothless beak, small crested skull, long neck, short torso, and long legs. It was small, with the [[holotype]] having an estimated body mass of between {{cvt|9|-|15|kg|lb}} based on the [[circumference]] of the {{dinogloss|femur}}, which is {{convert|18.5|cm|in}} long. Despite this small size, [[histological]] analysis of the femur, {{dinogloss|fibula}}, and {{dinogloss|metatarsal|second metatarsal}} revealed a series of closely spaced growth marks near the outer surface of the bones, indicative of an external fundamental system (a signal of skeletal maturity). The histology further suggests the animal was at least 6—probably 7—years old when it died, at which point it was fully grown. As such, ''Infernogallus'' is substantially smaller than the two other named Hell Creek caenagnathids: ''[[Eoneophron]]'', estimated to weigh {{convert|78|kg|lb}}, and ''[[Anzu wyliei|Anzu]]'', estimated at {{convert|202|-|342|kg|lb}}. === Skull === [[File:Infernogallus jamesi (holotype skull cropped).png|thumb|left|Photograph (a) and line drawing (b) of [[holotype]] skull as preserved and [[µCT]] renderings with (c) and without (d) mandible included]] The skull is highly modified compared to most other theropods, with several unusual traits. It is superficially most similar to that of [[oviraptorid]]s (the caenagnathid [[sister group]]), clearly distinct from that reconstructed for the more closely related ''Anzu''. As the skull anatomy of other eucaenagnathines is poorly documented, it is unclear whether much of this unique anatomy is unique to ''Infernogallus'' or typical of its relatives as well. Much of the unique anatomy concerns the side of the skull, the temporal region. The {{dinogloss|orbit}} (eye hole) is large and circular, taking up almost 40% of the skull's total length. Contrastingly, the {{dinogloss|infratemporal fenestra}} (a hole behind the orbit for jaw muscles) is extremely small, only 25% the diameter of the orbit. The {{dinogloss|jugal}} (a cheek bone forming the lower rim of the orbit) has been significantly reshaped by the large orbit and small infratemporal fenestra. Its overall shape is broad, unlike the thin rodlike structure seen in other oviraptorosaurs. Its front end forks into a forward-projecting process connecting to the {{dinogloss|maxilla}} (jawbone), more developed than in other oviraptorosaurs, and an upward-projecting process connecting to the {{dinogloss|lacrimal}} and forming part of the orbit's front edge. This lacrimal process is otherwise absent in all but the earliest oviraptorosaurs. The back end of the jugal (forming the front rim of the infratemporal fenestra) is very broad and, uniquely among oviraptorosaurs, makes contact with the {{dinogloss|squamosal}} bone. Behind the jugal, the {{dinogloss|quadratojugal}} has a large circular projection, while it is only a small tab in other oviraptorosaurs. This forms a large [[external ear canal]] along with the squamosal. The squamosal itself is broad top to bottom, and lacks the typical depression and ridge used to support [[adduction|adductor muscles]]. [[File:Infernogallus and Citipati Skulls.png|thumb|Reconstructed skulls of ''Infernogallus'' (left) and the oviraptorid ''[[Citipati]]'' (right); note the maxillovomeral protrusion (mvp) and pterygoid (pt), outlined in blue dotted line, as well as the position of the ''pterygoideus'' muscle (mPTv)]] As in other oviraptorosaurs, the {{dinogloss|palate}} (roof of the mouth) is highly modified. Oviraptorosaurs typically possess two prominent protrusions from the palate: a maxillovomeral process formed by the {{dinogloss|maxilla}} (jawbone) and the {{dinogloss|vomer}}, and one formed by the {{dinogloss|ectopterygoid}} and {{dinogloss|pterygoid}} bones. In ''Infernogallus'', both are exceptionally large, projecting far below the rest of the palate. The ectopterygoid-pterygoid bar in particular would have filled most of the [[oral cavity]]. In other oviraptorosaurs, the pterygoid only extends slightly downwards and has a small, narrow shelf at the bottom. In ''Infernogallus'', the pterygoid curves strongly downwards and has a long, broad shelf at its bottom. A prominent roughened pad termed the pterygoid buttress is present on the outer edge of the shelf. An earlier caenagnathid, ''[[Microvenator]]'', shows similar traits but in less extreme form. In particular, the size of the pterygoid shelf is much more developed in ''Infernogallus'' than in ''Microvenator'' with large depressions on the top and bottom for attachment of the ''pterygoideus'' muscles. The ectopterygoid, connecting the pterygoid and the jugal, is especially simplified and reduced compared to other oviraptorosaurs, whereas the {{dinogloss|palatine}} is especially robust and broad. [[File:Infernogallus jamesi (paratype mandible, NDGS 4351).png|thumb|left|Scan of paratype dentary (NDGS 4351)]] As in other caenagnathids, the left and right {{dinogloss|mandibles}} (low jaws) are fused and steeply upturned when seen from the side. This forms the animal's toothless beak, similar to living [[turtle]]s and [[bird]]s. The inside edge of the mandible bears prominent grooves and ridges, a key feature unique to caenagnathids. Amongst these was a large [[sulcus (morphology)|sulcus]] (groove) present over the {{dinogloss|mandibular symphysis}} (the point where the left and right mandibles meet), into which the maxillovomeral protrusion would have fit when the mouth was closed. Underneath the symphysis, there was a prominent insertion for the [[genioglossus]] muscle, likely supporting a powerful tongue. This insertion is W-shaped, unlike the heart or hourglass shape seen in other caegnathids. The 'chin' region of the dentary is round, similar to ''Chirostenotes'' but distinct from the more squared 'chins' of ''[[Leptorhynchos gaddisi|Leptorhynchos]]'' and ''Elmisaurus''. Like other caengnathids, there is a largely elliptical {{dinogloss|mandibular fenestra}} spanning around 35% of the length of the mandible. A deep [[wikt:fossa|fossa]] is present in front of the fenestra, and just below this is small, sideward-projecting [[tubercle (bone)|tubercle]] unseen in other caenagnathids. The {{dinogloss|articular}}, which forms the jaw joint with the {{dinogloss|quadrate}} bone of the skull, has a prominent rounded ridge that slots into the saddle-shaped ends of the quadrate, allowing forward and backward motion of the mandible. === Postcrania === {{multiple image | align = right | direction = horizontal | width = | header = | image1 = Infernogallus jamesi (holotype neck and body).png | image2 = Infernogallus jamesi (holotype hand and foot).png | footer = Holotype neck and body (left), hand (right, a–c), and foot (right, d) }} ''Infernogallus'' has a long neck, composed of twelve {{dinogloss|cervical vertebrae}} in addition to the {{dinogloss|atlas}} and {{dinogloss|axis}}, the first two vertebrae that serve to attach the head. The [[epipophyses]] (projecting muscle attachment points near the top of vertebrae) are very reduced compared to other oviraptorosaurs. As in birds and other theropods, the vertebrae are hollow, with extensive [[Skeletal pneumaticity|pneumatic]] air spaces. The torso, as in other caenagnathids, was rather short. The [[scapula|shoulder bone]] was thin and minimally expanded. As in other oviraptorosaurs, it bore a large {{dinogloss|acromion}}, an attachment point for a boomerang-shaped [[furcula]]. As in relatives such as ''[[Apatoraptor]]'' and ''Elmisaurus'', the arms inserted into the shoulder joint from the side, potentially allowing more arm motion. The large {{dinogloss|deltapectoral crest}} of the [[humerus|upper arm]] was shorter than that of some oviraptorids, and the [[ulna|lower arm]] bone was bowed instead of straight as in [[Heyuanninae|heyuannine]] oviraptorids. The hands were long and would have been able to grasp. The second {{dinogloss|metacarpal}} (hand bone) is the longest, and has a shallow ridge on its [[wikt:extensor|extensor]] surface absent in other caenagnathids. The fingers are similar in proportion to those of related caenagnathids such as ''Elmisaurus'' and ''[[Hagryphus]]'', and bear curved claws. The rear part of the {{dinogloss|ilium}} (part of the hip) is broken off, but the observable front half is lower than in ''Chirostenotes'' and ''[[Caenagnathus]]'', being more similar to ''Elmisaurus''. As a caenagnathid, ''Infernogallus'' has long limbs and long, splayed toes, with curved claws at their ends. Unlike in ''Elmisaurus'' and ''[[Citipes]]'', the foot bones were not extensively fused together. The tail is unpreserved, but is short in other caenagnathids. == Classification == [[File:Infernogallus jamesi.png|thumb|[[Life restoration]] of ''Infernogallus'']] [[File:Hell Creek Formation caenagnathids.png|thumb|Environmental reconstruction of three Hell Creek caenagnathids, including ''Eoneophron'' (top left) and ''Anzu'' (right)]] To test the affinities and relationships of ''Infernogallus'', Funston et al. (2026) included it in an extensively updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix of Funston et al. (2020). The exact interrelationships and resolution of caenagnathids varied based on the analytical methodologies used. Their time-scaled [[Bayesian inference in phylogeny|Bayesian]] tree recovered ''Infernogallus'' as the [[sister taxon]] to a clade including ''[[Epichirostenotes]]'', ''[[Elmisaurus]]'', and ''[[Citipes]]''. These 'elmisaurins' were recovered alongside several 'caenagnathins' (e.g., ''[[Anzu wyliei|Anzu]]'', ''[[Caenagnathus]]'', and ''[[Chirostenotes]]'') in a derived caenagnathid clade the authors called Eucaenagnathinae. Due to the instability and inconsistency of interrelationships, Funston and colleagues cautioned against formally establishing these subclades, but recognized the persistence of certain groupings. These results are displayed in the [[cladogram]] below. {{clade |{{clade |1=[[Oviraptoridae]] |label2=[[Caenagnathidae]] |2={{clade |1=''[[Microvenator]]'' |2={{clade |1=''[[Gigantoraptor]]'' |2={{clade |1=''[[Anomalipes]]'' |2={{clade |1=''[[Caenagnathasia]]'' |label2=[[Eucaenagnathinae]] |2={{clade |style1=background-color:#EDD7E7; |1={{clade |1=''[[Chirostenotes]]'' |2=''[[Hagryphus]]'' }} |3={{clade |style1=background-color:#EDD7E7; |1={{clade |1=''[[Apatoraptor]]'' |2={{clade |1=''[[Anzu wyliei|Anzu]]'' |2=''[[Caenagnathus]]'' }} }} |style3=background-color:#F7DFDA; |3={{clade |1=''[[Eoneophron]]'' |2={{clade |1='''''Infernogallus'''''

{{legend2|#F7DFDA}} 'elmisaurins' == Paleobiology == In their study of the inner ear of ''Infernogallus'', Bazzana‐Adams and colleagues recognized a relatively short [[cochlea]], consistent with reduced auditory sensitivity or discrimination compared to other theropods. If this is a widespread feature in caenagnathids, it seems to contradict the carnivorous ecology postulated for some species, which would benefit from enhanced hearing capabilities when seeking prey. [[File:Infernogallus jamesi (jaw motion).png|thumb|left|Reconstructed chewing stroke of ''Infernogallus'']] Several unique features of the jaw and [[Temporal fenestra|temporal region]] help to clarify the diet and functional morphology of ''Infernogallus''. The muscles associated with the palate are enlarged, while those associated with the temporal region are reduced, indicative of a weaker bite force than non-caenagnathid oviraptorosaurs. The arrangement of the {{dinogloss|quadrate}} and {{dinogloss|articular}} (upper and lower jaw bones comprising the jaw joint) indicates that the lower jaw would be able to slide forward, up to ~14% of the skull length. Finally, the [[Occlusion (dentistry)|occlusal]] surfaces of the jaws would have been highly textured in life, allowing for the effective crushing and shearing of soft foods. This would be aided by the strong tongue, as suggested by the muscle insertion site on the mandible. Enhanced tongue mobility in caenagnathids is suggested by the relatively long {{dinogloss|hyoids}} (not preserved in ''Infernogallus''), as in modern birds with mobile tongues. Taken together, these features suggest a highly specialized chewing stroke and food processing mechanism in ''Infernogallus''. This contrasts with more '[[Primitive (phylogenetics)|primitive]]' oviraptorosaurs (e.g., ''[[Caudipteryx]]'') which lack these features and likely relied on a high-[[fiber]] plant diet, the digestion of which was facilitated by the intake of [[gastroliths]]. The body cavity of ''Infernogallus'' is complete and articulated, including the complete {{dinogloss|gastralia|gastral basket}}, but no gastroliths are evident, suggesting they were not involved in this species' digestion. Some adaptations for [[durophagy]] (consuming hard-shelled animals) are seen in oviraptorids, but not in caenagnathids. Caenagnathids thus likely relied on a non-fibrous, soft diet that still required oral processing and manipulation. [[File:1 pesquet's parrot bird paradise 2025.jpg|thumb|''Infernogallus'' may have eaten fruit in a way similar to Pesquet's parrot]] The closest living analog to the skull structure and muscle functions of ''Infernogallus'' is [[Pesquet's parrot]] (''Psittrichas fulgidus''). This parrot is adapted to [[frugivory]] (fruit eating), which it does by eating the pulp and discarding the seed. Most other parrots are [[granivorous]], targeting the seed. The comparatively longer and lower skull and mandible of ''P. fuldigus'' are reminiscent of the skull modifications of caenagnathids like ''Infernogallus'' compared to other oviraptorosaurs. Fossil evidence suggests caenagnathids originated soon after [[angiosperm]] fruits, including those with a single internal seed surrounded by a fleshy [[mesocarp]] (called [[drupes]]). The oldest and earliest-diverging caenagnathid, ''[[Microvenator]]'', exhibits some of the adaptations for oral processing seen in ''Infernogallus''. It is thus possible that the increasingly derived jaw and palate structure of caenagnathids paralleled the diversification of drupes in the Late Cretaceous. Overall, ''Infernogallus'' was likely frugivorous, engaging in fruit defleshing, as in Pesquet's parrot. == See also == * [[Timeline of oviraptorosaur research]] * [[Paleobiota of the Hell Creek Formation]] == References == {{Reflist|refs= {{Cite journal |last1=Funston |first1=Gregory F. |last2=Dudgeon |first2=Thomas W. |last3=Simon |first3=D.
